Gwynedd
GWIN-eth
n. (the mountain princedom of north Wales, seat of the see of Bangor and the last Welsh power to fall to Edward I)
Welsh Gwynedd, probably from the same root as the Irish Féni, the Goidelic settlers; the Latin form is Venedotia.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gwynedd is the north-western princedom of Wales, holding Snowdonia and the coastal plain behind it, and its mountains made it the last Welsh power to be reduced. Its princes claimed descent from Cunedda; Rhodri Mawr, Llywelyn ap Iorwerth and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd ruled from Aberffraw and Dolwyddelan, and the independence of native Wales ended with Llywelyn's death in 1282 and the castles Edward I raised at Caernarfon, Conwy and Harlech. The see of Bangor, founded by Deiniol in the sixth century, is the ecclesiastical centre; its cathedral was burned more than once in the wars and rebuilt poorly, and the diocese was among the poorest in the kingdom, so that its parishes were commonly held by absentees and served by curates who could barely live. That poverty is the key to the Reformation's slow progress in the north: the Welsh Bible of 1588 was law, but a book needs a reader and a preacher needs a stipend. The change came late and came from below, through the schools and then through the Calvinistic Methodist exhorters; Thomas Charles of Bala, in the old Gwynedd country, organised the supply of Welsh Bibles, and John Elias preached across Anglesey and Caernarfonshire with great effect. The dictionary records the mountains as a shelter and refuses to make them a merit.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a mountain as a large mass of earth rising above the common level; a see as the seat of episcopal power; a curate as one employed to perform the duties of another; a fastness as a stronghold; and a stipend as a settled pay.

expand to see more

MOUNTAIN, n. A large mass of earth and rock, rising above the common level of the earth or of adjacent land.

SEE, n. The seat of episcopal power; the diocese or jurisdiction of a bishop.

CURATE, n. A clergyman employed to perform the duties of another; one who has the cure of souls.

FASTNESS, n. A strong hold; a fortress or fort; a place of defence difficult of access.

STIPEND, n. Settled pay or compensation for services, whether daily, monthly or annual.

Key Scripture

Psa 125:2 — "As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever."

Pro 18:10 — "The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe."

Jer 3:15 — "And I will give you pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding."

Mic 6:9 — "The LORD'S voice crieth unto the city, and the man of wisdom shall see thy name: hear ye the rod, and who hath appointed it."

Modern Corruption

North Welsh princedom whose mountains preserved a native power until 1282 and whose poor see of Bangor left the Reformation to be carried by schools and preachers rather than by endowment.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the trust men put in a strong country. Gwynedd was defensible, and its defensibility bred a confidence that outlasted the thing defended; the hills held off armies for eight centuries and could not hold off one judgment. Scripture allows the comfort and relocates it: the mountains are a figure of the LORD's own keeping, for “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people” (Psa 125:2), and the only fastness that cannot be taken is a name, since “The name of the LORD is a strong tower: the righteous runneth into it, and is safe” (Pro 18:10). Caernarfon was built precisely to prove that rock is not refuge.

A second and quieter corruption belongs to the dictionary's own side of the account, and is named as ours. A reformed establishment held the see of Bangor for two centuries while leaving it too poor to be preached in, filling it with men who drew the title elsewhere and left the cure to a curate; the promise God makes is of “pastors according to mine heart, which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding” (Jer 3:15), and a diocese administered as a source of revenue has not received them. The rod spoke before the remedy came, for the LORD's “voice crieth unto the city” (Mic 6:9), and the remedy, when it came, came through Bala and the schools and not through the bishops.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew har (H2022), a mountain; Hebrew sabib (H5439), round about; Hebrew ra'ah (H7462), to feed as a shepherd.

expand to see more

Hebrew har (H2022) — a mountain, a hill country; “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem”, Psalm 125:2.

Hebrew sabib (H5439) — round about, encircling; “so the LORD is round about his people”, Psalm 125:2.

Hebrew migdal (H4026) — a tower, a raised stronghold; “The name of the LORD is a strong tower”, Proverbs 18:10.

Hebrew ra'ah (H7462) — to tend, to pasture, to feed a flock; “pastors according to mine heart”, Jeremiah 3:15.

Hebrew de'ah (H1844) — knowledge; “which shall feed you with knowledge and understanding”, Jeremiah 3:15.

Usage

"“As the mountains are round about Jerusalem” (Psa 125:2) — Snowdonia as the shelter of the princes."

"“The name of the LORD is a strong tower” (Pro 18:10) — the castles of 1283 against the only true fastness."

"“pastors according to mine heart” (Jer 3:15) — the want of them in the poor see of Bangor."
